DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: S continuation of the Black Feather vein system, Vertical quartz-siderite lode to 6m wide with malachite, bornite, chalcopyrite in host shale of the Bunyeroo Formation. Reported production to 1907 was ~ 163t including ~19t treated ore at 5-9%Cu.

Cu mineralisation in a NS-trending qz-siderite vein system in host slate of the Bunyeroo Formation. Production to 1899 was ~14t ore @ 4-16% Cu, though a 1909 report indicated ""considerable"" ore raised.
MINEROLOGY_GANGUE: Barite,  Calcite,  Iron oxide (non specific),  Quartz,  Siderite

DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: aeromagnetic anomaly, of ~25km strike length at SW end of Karari Fault Zone. Drilling identified magnetite-bearing intervals of gneiss, with assays to 27%Fe. Preliminary resource estimate for 5km strike 180Mtonne at 16.6%Fe, for mt conc 70.5%Fe.

stream sediment sampling returned heavy mineral contents high in rare earths. Heavy mineral fraction ~38% of the total, with zircon content to 1.6-8.6 %, TIO2 content 1.5 to 8.9%. REE of yttrium 100 ppm, cerium 800 ppm, and lanthanum at 600 ppm.

1970s exploration by Australian Aquitaine Petroleum Pty Ltd in the area of Mengersons Well identified several shows of copper carbonate and copper oxide minerals associated with quartz veining related to intrusions of mafic dykes.

oxidised copper mineralisation, with rare disseminated copper sulphides found at a faulted contact between gneiss of the Birksgate Complex, and sediment of the Moorilyanna Graben. Assays returned up to 2%Cu, with trace Ag.
Cu mineralisation adjacent to mafic dyke at faulted contact of Birksgate Complex and Adelaidean sediments. Rock chip samples returned assays to 600ppmCu, 550ppmPb, rare anomalous Au.
small prospecting pits dug by L.A. Wells in 1903 near a water well on Granite Downs Station on a pyritic quartz reef in host Waturu Gneiss. Grab samples for assay returned trace gold.

quartz vein carried copper minerals. The vein cross cut slate of the Rodda Beds. The vein was ~100m long by 25cm wide, with iron oxide and pyrite visible, along with malachite. Assays revealed no gold.
lateritised, silicified ultramafic host with minor green chrysoprase. There were relict olivine textures, with elevated nickel recorded in minor veinlets of secondary chrysoprase.
copper mineralisation associated with fractures, and joint planes in a metasomatised dolerite dyke. The dyke cross cut ultramafic rocks. Rare chalcopyrite was noted.
ironstone gossan, with anomalous Ni-Cu-Co, with drilling identifying serpentine after olivine rock, with minor disseminated sulphides, including pentlandite.

malachite, and chalcopyrite, associated with calcite-bearing lenses in a variably sheared older EW-trending gabbro dyke intruding metasediment of the Birksgate Complex. The lenses and veins were comprised largely of calcite and epidote.

malachite, and chalcopyrite, associated with calcite-bearing lenses in a variably sheared older EW-trending gabbro dyke intruding metasediment of the Birksgate Complex. The lenses and veins were comprised largely of calcite and epidote.

profile of jasper developed over serpentinite of the Giles Complex, reconnaissance geological assessment by Wightman and Taylor in the early 1970s identified possibly prospective for nickel at depth, though not sampled.

nickeliferous rock recorded during field mapping on the Kokatara 50K map. Occurrence was associated with ultrabasic rock of the Giles Complex, though no sampling, and hence no actual values for elevated Ni were recorded.
small outcrops of dolomitic jasper, possibly the surface expression of ultra basic rocks.
surace jasper with elevated Ni values as surface expression of serpentine at depth, with potential for primary nickel. see Eateringinna 1:50,000 Geological  Atlas Series.

outcrop of subcropping jasper identified during mapping, and thought to be derived from a serpentinite, and with potential for nickel mineralisation. Not drill ested, no surface sampling and geochemistry completed.

outcrop of rubbly, nodular dolomite, thought to indicate ultramafic rock at depth. The dolomite capping carried anomalous Ni and Cr. Follow up drilling confirmed the presence of basic rock at depth, but no nickel sulphides were recorded.
jasper outcrop developed over subcropping serpentinite. Samples returned minor nickel anomalism to 1900 ppm.
Cu-Ni mineralisation in ochre/jasper bodies after serpentinite. Best drill analysis value 9.8m @ 0.41%Cu in a zone of disseminated chalcopyrite and pyrite 5m wide by 430m long.

secondary copper mineralisation recorded in fractures, with minor chalcopyrite in host metasediment and dolerite. Geophysical exploration determined the presence of an associated low grade IP and geochemistry anomaly trending NS.

disseminated Cu sulphides associated with lens of basic granulite in keel of tight syncline, and minor mineraisation within Giles Complex intrusive. Best values from granulite were 10 rock chip samples >1000ppm, 1 sample >5,000ppm.
norite body in Birksgate Complex that was prospected for nickel.
ultra basic body within Birksgate Complex gneiss that was prospected for nickel. Tested in a diamond drill hole which confirmed a norite/olivine norite, with only low levels of pyrite.

basic granulite of the Giles Complex carrying minor copper carbonate in joint fractures. The associated quartzo-feldspathic gneiss trended NS, dipped 50 W. There was a weak IP anomaly following down dip.
narrow body of dolomite, and weakly magnetic jasper suspected of capping a serpentinised ultramafic rock. It carried elevated nickel and chromium values, with no visible sulphides.
thick capping of jasper rock over serpentinite/ultra basic rock, with drilling returning samples assaying to 6000 ppm Ni, averaging 2000 ppm.
weathered cap developed on serpentinite with anomalous nickel. One sample of nickeliferous vermiculite @ 3.2% Ni. Underlying serpentinite recorded much lower Ni values.
small jasper occurrence checked for nickel content. Results were poor. Some pits were dug seeking chrysoprase. See Witjuti SADME 1:50,000 Geological Atlas Series.

lenticular body of serpentine capped with jasper, and concordant with gneiss. Sampling from pits returned 1600 ppm Ni. Body associated with strong magnetic anomaly, apparently due to bordering, concordant pyroxene-magnetite quartzite.

largest intrusion in the Musgrave Ranges, being rectangular in shape over an area of 10,400 hectares. Mapping identified disseminated chalcopyrite deposited in weathered norite located at the east end of the intrusion mass.
dolomitic and siliceous caprock on weathered ultramafics. Sampling identified best values 1700ppmNi, 2000ppmCr.

drilling of a mafic igneous complex of the Giles Complex identified magnetite-rich intervals associated with trace primary chalcopyrite & pentlandite. Probable middle to upper part of layered mafic/ultramafic intrusive that reached sulphur saturation.
vanadium-titanium occurrence was an area of isolated, lenticular magnetite bodies, up to 2m thick, within a sequence carrying vanadium to 1.26%, and titanium to 10%.

veins of chrysoprase to 5cm wide, and of poor quality, and varied colour. Thinner veins of dark green varieties occurred in hard jasper further up the creek. Minor 12 mm wide veins of chromite was recorded.
surface show of chrysoprase tested at depth in diamond drill hole DDHA 14, with chrysoprase veinlets encountered sporadically to 200 m depth in host Giles Complex mafic igneous rock.

rare gem quality chrysoprase and trace moss agate (chalcedony with manganese and iron oxide dendrites) and veins of white to translucent chalcedony occurred as irregular masses and veinlets in nickeliferous ochre and jasper deposits.

rare gem quality chrysoprase and trace moss agate (chalcedony with manganese and iron oxide dendrites) and veins of white to translucent chalcedony occurred as irregular masses and veinlets in nickeliferous ochre and jasper deposits.

clusters to 1-3 m long of celestite crystals were found. Two localities 400 m apart were sampled returning values of > 90% SRSO4.
small veins and vughs of celestite within an ironstone. One vein was 2 m long by 2 cm thick.
float and outcropping vein celestite to 2 cm thick assaying 92.8% SrSO4.
crystalline fragments collected from veins, that assayed 73.9% SRSO4 and 23.1%  BASO4.
quartz sands cemented by celestite, with float extending for 86 m and outcropping over 15 m. Grab sample assayed 85.9% SrSO4.
surface float of veins of celestite in ironstone. Drilling failed to intersect subsurface veins.
2 areas of float consisting of crystals of celestite. Assays were to <60% SrSO4.
3 adjacent roadside pits on deposit of Holocene white clay, and excavated for road making material. One large pit, 2 smaller for total area >20,000m2 x 1-2m deep.
thin slabs of crystalline celestite from veins roughly parallel to bedding of host sediments assayed  73.9% SrSO4 and 23.1% BaSO4.
thin slabs of crystalline celestite from veins roughly parallel to bedding of host sediments assayed  91% SrSO4 AND 93% SrSO4.

thin slabs of crystalline celestite from veins roughly parallel to bedding of host sediments assayed  86.4% SrSO4 AND 96% SrSO4.
small veins of celestite in Wooldridge Limestone Member, and minor float.

113t celestite (SrSO4) mined in 1928, & from 1940-41for recovery of 113 tonne. Occurred as loose blocks in sand, and in veins in Cretaceous limestone host.  Exploration in 1969-70 failed to locate significant resource.
shallow quarry of dimensions <10,000m2 x 1-4m deep developed for road fill, and located on the eastern flank of the prominent landform of McDouall Peak comprising weathered Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.

outcrop of altered Hiltaba granite. Main supply of road metal for Coober Pedy township. Used as rail ballast for Adelaide-Darwin railroad. Production from 1988-2009 ~77,000t. Small resource of overlying ornamental ironstone stockpiled.
estimated 50,000m3 of altered Hiltaba granite quarried for road metal. Large stockpile of aggregate partially consumed in 2008-9 for road making. Open cut partly rehabilitated.

opal occurred in the shale at ""levels"" and ""slides."" Workings consisted of two bulldozer cuts to 5 m depth, some hand dug shallow shafts, and caldwell drill holes to 10 m depth. Alunite was recorded.
few bulldozer scrapes on bleached weathered shales of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale. The precious opal occurred in the shale at levels and slides. Gypsum and alunite was common.

small field developed in 1969, with bulldozer cuts to 7m concentrated in one area. Isolated shafts to 13m. Active from 1971-72 producing good parcels of opal. Host was bleached shales and some coarser sandstone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.

group of bulldozer cuts and backhoe trenches excavated for precious opal. Host was bleached claystone of Cretaceous Bulldog Shale, with minor thin sandy interbeds. Overlain by younger Tertiary red alluvium and calcrete of Russo Beds.
small field worked extensively from the mid 1960's to 8m depth predominantly via bulldozer cuts, and scattered underground workings to 13m.
small field of bulldozer cuts to 7m maximum depth, and shafts with some driving at depths of 10-13m. Opal occurred in shales as levels and slides, with gypsum and alunite common.

small field opened in 1964 on Bulldog Shale. Workings consisted of bulldozer cuts to 6m below a scarp. Underground workings developed on top of the scarp, possibly working the same levels at 15 m depth. There was some activity in 1978-79.

small field opened in 1972. Scattered cuts to 8m along a creek, with underground workings occurring discontinuously to E for ~6km to Dead Mans Gully. One area of extensive machine tunnelling was to 15m. Active 1980-81. Host was Bulldog Shale.

small field of scattered hand-dug to Calweld shafts, with some backfilled trenches. Main activity 1976 on finds of floaters, only trace opal recovered. Host was bleached weathered shales with minor coarser sands of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.

2 bulldozer cuts, 2m deep in 1980. On the surrounds Calweld shafts to 10m. Nearby subsidised shafts with level at 9m. There were deeper shafts uphill to the NE and SE. Host was bleached weathered shales of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.

small field opened 1986. Opal found by deepening of old shaft onto level at 17m. Subsidised Shaft 156 found opal 400 m to the west. Host rock was bleached shales and some coarser sandstone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.
developed in the mid 1960's as a small field with mainly underground workings along levels 14-17 m deep. Opal was found in host bleached claystone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.
established in mid 1960's. Underground workings developed on higher ground mostly to 10-14, some to 18 m. Bulldozer cuts located to west 6-11 m deep. Jasper (hard Russo Beds) were very common.

precious opal found in 1946. There was major activity in 1958 with some large finds then sporadic activity since. Underground workings on higher ground on levels to 16-22 m. Some bulldozer cuts established downhill on S and N margins.
scattered small workings consisted of bulldozer cuts and underground workings, mostly shallow (5-I I m deep), with some underground workings to maximum depth of 17 m.
extensive diggings developed in 1963 with precious opal recovered from levels 14-19m deep, all from underground workings.
small field established in 1986 consisting of a group of underground workings 12-14 m deep.

underground workings, with levels 15-20 m deep. it was active during 1981-82. Host rock was bleached weathered shales with minor coarser sands of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale were overlain by younger red alluvium of the Russo Beds.
bulldozer cuts exposed levels at 4-9 m depth. Host rock was bleached weathered shales with minor coarser sands of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale were overlain by younger red alluvium of the Russo Beds.
workings for precious opal over a small area, with several areas of bulldozer cuts to maximum depth of 7 m with underground workings slightly uphill to the east, driving along a depth of 8 m.
discovered in 1964, workings were mostly bulldozer cuts to maximum depth of 9 m, with minor underground workings. The major activity was in 1979-81.

established in early 1960s. Merged with Prospect Field to N, and Emu Flat Field to S. Opal found initially in shallow ground. Extensive dozer cuts to 6-9m, underground on higher ground to W, levels 12-18m. Surge in operations in 1984.
extensive opal workings opened in 1964, worked extensively 1978-79, 1981-82. Northern part was all underground workings 15-20m deep, western end, 12-18m deep.
or Seven Mile, in 1957. Underground workings in the northern part of the field had levels 14-18 m deep. Shallower underground and open-cut workings were located on lower ground to the south.
extensive diggings developed in 1946 on levels and slides in host bleached weathered shale/siltstone of the Bulldog Shale. Area was renowned for the quality and abundance of opal.

precious opal of high quality, found in levels, in horizontal cracks (some vertical also), or on the lower contact between thin sandy interbeds and claystone. Minor Alunite and gypsum also present. Host was bleached claystone of the Bulldog Shale.

established in mid 1960s, large and productive field, with reputation for good opal. Mostly underground, some bulldozer cuts. Levels at 14-19m. Field extended W following discovery of Southern Cross field. Southwards extension was unlikely.
workings in bleached Bulldog Shale and some coarser sands, overlain by younger red alluvial Russo Beds. Opal occurred in shales as levels and slides. Gypsum and alunite were common.

several areas of bulldozer cuts 6-10 m deep, with extensive auger drilling were developed in 1973. The Quail field had cuts to 7 m maximum depth, and some shafts with drives at about 15 m. It was active during 1981-82.

opal workings opened in 1964 on bleached Bulldog Shale, overlain by younger red alluvial Russo Beds. Opal occurred in shales as levels and slides. Gypsum and alunite was common. It was a small field with shallow bulldozer cuts to maximum 7 m depth.
workings scattered along a scarp southwest of Shellpatch, with a second group 2 km west of Shellpatch. Workings consisted of bulldozer cuts, backhoe trenches and hand-dug shafts to 7 m depth.

2 groups of workings, W of Stuart Highway, being underground workings to 20m, and dozer cuts. Also E of Stuart Highway (Whiskey), backhoe trenches and dozer cuts to 6m. Worked as early as 1923, major operations 1962-63. Some dugouts.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: HARD HILL; NINETEEN MILE; TWENTY MILE; YELLOW HILL
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: or 20 Mile established in 1921. Host Bulldog Shale. 20 mile referred to W end of Vino field. This area consisted of extensive bulldozed cuts around the base of scarps, with backhoe pits on the flat area below, and a few shafts on top of the scarp.

numerous pits and dozer cuts to 4-5m on the flat and on the scarp, few shafts on top of scarp. Other cuts scattered around mesas for about 1km E & W of the main workings. The eastern workings are within an area reserved from mining.

developed in the mid 1960s. Large field, which merged with Vino Field to W and 14 Mile to S. Mainly underground workings on several levels at ~21m, some deep dozer cuts. E underground workings and cuts to 15-18m. Considerable activity in 1978-79.

important field discovered early on. Major dozing in 1968. Underground workings to 18-22m on the higher ground. It was consistently active with surges of mining during 1978-79 and 1981. Later activity in the NW corner.
developed in 1970. Very small field consisting of a group of backhoe pits near a track to the Breakaways lookout, and a single bulldozer cut I km to the southwest. Only traces of opal were found.

started in 1948. Workings were mainly bulldozer cuts, to maximum 9 m depth, obscuring older shallow workings. Some underground workings took place on higher ground in the southeastern and southwestern margins to 18 m depth.

established in 1963. Large field, said to be a reliable producer of opal, but of generally below average quality. Field mainly underground workings, with levels 18-23m. Some cuts and backhoe trenches were located  in shallower ground down scarp.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: AVLIS; NINE MILE; STEINBISS; STONY HILL
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: established in 1964. Large field with several areas underground workings to 17-22m, dozer cuts and trenches below. Merged with Greek Gully to the NW. Major activity in 1978-79 with operations in 1983 being along the scarp south of the main workings.
2 bulldozer cuts with some shafts nearby and other scattered shafts. Subsidised shafts found good sandstone.

intensive shallow workings adjacent to Stuart Highway of backhoe pits and cuts, mostly less than 4m, with few shafts to 7m. Most opal was alluvial. There were some cuts on a scarp 1.5 km to the southwest. It was active during 1973-74.
opened in 1964 over a small area. Workings were bulldozer cuts to 13 m depth on a scarp, and some old underground workings. There were several dugouts.

developed in 1971 as intensively bulldozed area along a scarp, with underground workings up the scarp to the SW along levels 17-19m deep. Some underground workings located west of the Stuart Highway. It was active during 1976-77 and 1978-80.
developed in 1971 for precious opal over a small area. Host rock was bleached shales and some coarser sandstone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.
small group of underground workings in levels about 20 m deep. Precious opal was found in host bleached claystone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.

group of workings for precious opal over a small area. Host rock was bleached shales and some coarser sandstone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale, overlain by younger red alluvium , and off-white calcrete of the Tertiary Russo Beds.

group of workings establihed in 1939l. Workings consisted of deep shafts hand dug to a maximum depth of 23 m on top of a hill. There was extensive driving. Shallower underground and some bulldozer workings occurred down on the scarp.

opal as seams and in levels in host weathered Cretaceous Bulldog Shale. Discovered 1915, now original field largely destroyed by dozer trenching. Subsequently the Coober Pedy Precious Stones Field was declared & became largest producer of precious opal in the world.
one of the original opal diggings opened in 1915-16. It is now within the town area, and mining is not permitted. Dugouts and roads have obscured most workings.
one of the original group of workings for precious opal over a small area in 1915-16. it is now within town area and mining is not permitted. Dugouts and roads have obscured most workings.
one of the original group of workings for precious opal over a small area in 1915-16. it is now within town area and mining is not permitted. Dugouts and roads have obscured most workings.

opened in 1964 being a small field in host bleached Bulldog Shale. It consisted of several deep bulldozer cuts around a scarp, and a few old hand-dug shafts. There were several dugouts. It is now within the town area.
established in the mid 1960s. Bulldozer cuts were located around a scarp, with a few shafts on top of scarp having levels to 20 m. There were several dugouts. It now lies within the town area.
established in 1918 as group of hand-dug workings then largely bulldozed about 1970. The opal was found in cuts 2-3 m above the old workings. It now lies within the town area.

small area of cuts and underground workings, 14-17 m deep, on higher ground. It was active during 1979-80. It is now in the town area. Host rock was bleached shales and some coarser sandstone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale.
found in 1920. The workings consisted of scattered, shallow bulldozer cuts around scarp margins. The area is now mostly within the town area.
small field of opal workings established in 1964. It consisted of scattered shallow bulldozer cuts of 4-5 m depth and some dugouts. It is now partly within the town area.
diggings developed in bleached bulldog shales overlain by younger red alluvium Russo Beds. Opal occurred in shales as levels and slides. Gypsum and alunite was common.

diggings opened in 1964 in bleached bulldog shales, overlain by younger red alluvium Russo Beds. Opal occurred in shales as levels and slides. Gypsum and alunite were common. It was a small field on an isolated mesa east of the main scarp.
diggings for opal on bleached Bulldog Shale plotted from mine symbol on 1:250K Geology map sheet.
opal diggings developed on bleached Bulldog Shale.
diggings for opal developed on bleached Bulldog Shale silicified to porcellanite.
6 small groups of diggings for opal on Bulldog Shale, and within a two km radius. It was likely that no precious opal was recovered.
diggings for opal located from a mine symbol plotted on the 1:250K geology map.
diggings on bleached Bulldog Shale, with some precious opal seen on dumps.
small group of diggings for opal on Bulldog Shale.

diggings for opal scattered along a scarp of silcrete trending NW, and developed over bleached Cretaceous Bulldog Shale. Good opal was reported at shallow depths, and was said to have been coated with iron oxides, and difficult to recognise.

discovered in 1947, worked in the 1970's to depths of ~6m, with ""Painted Ladies"" being a feature. Activity increased in 2004 with discovery of opal several m below traditional level in vertical seams.

N workings, Opal Valley, numerous shallow pits, dozer cuts on and below scarp, few underground workings on the W margin ~10m deep. Some painted ladies reported. Also Tee Valley, S workings, scattered cuts, backhoe pits to 10m on scarp.

as infillings at various depths to 30 m in horizontal structures, and in vertical and inclined joints, also following bedding planes. Best results at intersections of structures. Workings consisted initially of bulldozer cuts, later moving underground.

as infillings at various depths to 30 m in horizontal structures, and in vertical and inclined joints, and also following bedding planes. Best results at intersections of structures. Workings initially dozer cuts, later moving to underground operations.

as infillings at various depths to 30 m in horizontal structures, and in vertical and inclined joints, and also following bedding planes. Best results at intersections of structures. Workings initially dozer cuts, later moving to underground operations.

as infillings at various depths to 30 m in horizontal structures, and in vertical and inclined joints, and also following bedding planes. Best results at intersections of structures. Workings initially dozer cuts, later moving to underground operations.

major workings in Palaeozoic rocks. Opal occurred as infillings at various depths to 30 m in horizontal structures and in vertical and inclined joints, also following bedding planes. Best results were at the intersections of two of these structures.

opal found in host Ordovician kaolinitic sandstone as seams in horizontal or arcuate levels, or infilling steeply dipping verticals to depths of 25m. Fist discovered by Aboriginals World War 1, subsequently opened up in the 1920's.
massive vein of specular hematite developed within a fault in host Cambrian metasediment. There was some sampling from shallow pits. It was identified during regional mapping.
vein of specular hematite following the trend of a fault in Neoproterozoic Chambers Bluff Tillite .
diggings on host silcrete capping deeply weathered basement for recovery of average grade precious opal.

diggings on weathered shale of the Corunna Conglomerate, with sandy interbeds of silicified sandstone capping. Veins of blue potch and honey potch were reported. The opal was discovered in 1906, and worked further from 1955-1965.

2 opal diggings were developed on infilled fractures in deeply weathered gneiss, which trended NE and dipped 70 NW at the base of a silcrete-capped mesa. A trace of coloured potch was found on the mine dumps. There was no recorded production.

veins infilling fractures in host weathered Proterozoic crystalline basement rock. Precious opal as patches in thin veins, seams and lenses. Some precious opal was found on the dumps indicating some opal production.

opal in bedding plane partings and vertical joints in Wallatinna Formation. Small quantities found as cement to kaolinised, sandstone/conglomerate. The restricted area of kaolin distribution was seen as an indication that opal distribution was limited.

opal associated with weathered Bulldog Shale occurring as seams, & infilling cracks around nodules, as infilling of moulds replacing fossils, also opalised sandstone. Opal included high quality white (light), & crystal opal displaying good colour.
bleached claystone of the Bulldog Shale with coarse sandy interbeds, silicified and cemented in part by an opalised, 'coloured concrete'.
bulldozer cuts excavated to fresher brown claystone. Some basal quartzite boulders were seen in the mine dumps. The opal occurred below the sand lenses and/or at an arcuate joint or level.
diggings on weathered Bulldog Shale. Opal occurred in horizontal and vertical joints, the latter with silicified grey clays. Some good colour was found on the dumps.

weathered Bulldog Shale, with silcrete capped mesa host to rare precious opal. Pits exposed vertical and horizontal joints with white alunite and yellow brown smectite. One sample from the mine dumps included a vein with `colour.?
3 groups of opal workings on Bulldog Shale, and within 1km radius. Some of the silicification was opaline, as indicated from dump material. One prominent gypsum level was apparent.
precious opal in host bleached claystone of the Cretaceous Bulldog Shale, with some sandy interbeds up to 2 cms thick, both capped by porcellanite (silicified claystone).

opal in bleached claystone of Bulldog Shale with coarse sand interbeds. Upper part silicified, and overlain by red colluvial silt. Precious opal was found as cement surrounding sand grains, or as veins and lenses in the claystone.
historic opal diggings as dozer trenches and shafts on weathered Bulldog Shale, with workings distributed alongside dirt road for NS distance of >2km.
opal diggings in bleached weathered shales and sands with Tertiary capping, containing some opal.

opal diggings in Bulldog Shale, being white silty claystone overlain by up to 1 m of red silt. There was some silcrete capping. Black opal production was recorded. The opal was presumed to occur in levels and verticals as at Coober Pedy.
shallow shaft to 6m developed on a trace of copper carbonate disseminated in quartzite, and purple shale of the Pandurra Formation. Located near the boundary with overlying Woocalla Dolomite.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: KOSTERS PREMIER POTTERY; ML 2628; S.A. POTTERIES LTD; WOOCALLA CLAY
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: from 1920-1976, kaolin & illite clays from bleached zone of a silcrete profile mined for pottery and porcelain ware. Production from 1931-76 11,805t. Resources in 1981 were estimated at 27,000t.

quarry on Woocalla Dolomite. Production 1957-1980 ~405,000m3. Resource ~800m SE of ~300,000m3. Originally operated for rail ballast. Scalps used for road-base and sealing aggregate, also crushed as unders to ballast production.
Pleistocene freshwater limestone tested for suitability as a ballast resource. Resources of low grade material of ~240,000m3.
pit developed on river gravels for use as ballast. Estimated resource 500,000m3 in 1972, although 70% was undersize. Production from 1989-200137 >15,000 tonne gravel for concrete aggregate.
outcrop of Tertiary Mount Willoughby limestone tested for potential as ballast. Drilling and sampling identified a resource of low-grade material of 100,000m3 to 4m depth.

major quarry developed in late 1970s on quartzite to supply material for ballast and road aggregate. Production ~300,000m3 ballast, 182,000m3 scalps and screenings. Resource estimate for deepening by 15m 270,000m3.

37m wide dolerite dyke investigated for suitability for use as railway ballast, and tested in 1972 with 5 diamond core holes completed. Resource estimated at >300,000m3 to 20m depth, with potential a larger resource.
outcrop of rhyolite examined as a potential source of railway ballast.Resources estimated in 1972 at 500,000m3 to 20m depth
geophysical anomaly drill tested in hole 83MKRC-11, intercepting graphitic metasediment with 31.2m @ 7.1%C including 8m @ 11.8%C.

geophysics identified anomalous electromagnetics. It was subsequently drill tested, confirming graphitic metasediment. Best assay interval was hole 82MKD-13 with 36.4 m @ 2.9% C including 1.1 m @ 12.5% C.
electromagnetic anomaly identified several 100's metres to the south of Uley Mine. Drilling in 2007 confirmed narrow lenses of graphitic schist with grade to 14.5% organic carbon.

minor production of ~118 tonnes of magnesite from surface workings. Massive irregular blocks of magnesite were derived mainly by alteration of graphitic schist in situ, with some mobilisation features seen.
pegged but not worked (RB 85/62). Massive irregular blocks of magnesite were derived mainly by alteration of graphitic schist in situ, with some mobilisation features seen.

massive irregular blocks of magnesite derived mainly by alteration of schist of the Katunga Dolomite. Worked in 1916 for 102 t of sorted ore, grade 97.25%Mg, 1.9%SiO2. Zone ~100m long x 40m wide. Possible large resource.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: MC 16130; MC 2178; MC 2179; ML 2290; SECTION 6B; TUMBY BAY MAGNESITE
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: 3 trenches on masses of magnesite rock extending for 400m along strike, and up to 50m wide in host dolomite of the Hutchison Group. Production from 1915-1923 ~309 tonne. Remaining resources limited.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: EDWARDS CLAIM YARANYACKA; EDWARDS TALC; LOCATION 28; MC 618; MC 619
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: small quantity of flake graphite recorded in a graphite schist trending 040 . It was exposed in a shallow pit. The quantity of flake present was small, and flake size was almost microscopic.
historic quarry developed on deeply weathered metasediment for kaolin, with some graphite reported.

irregular masses of magnesite, with some associated graphite, trace copper carbonate. Massive nodules and boulders of magnesite. Below the magnesite some flake graphite (<6%) was recorded. Host mapped as Lower Middleback Jaspilite.
occurrence of disseminated to flake graphite in limonitic schist.
small elongate lenses to 2m wide of high grade magnesite mined in 1917 for 280 tonne. Host schist of the Hutchison Group. Band of graphitic schist, flake graphite content was 4% assaying 41%C.
host grey, gritty schist, with minor graphite as a coating, and a trace of flake graphite.
ironstone (possibly lateritised banded iron formation) that trended NNE, and carried some amorphous and flake graphite. One sample assayed  3.37% flake C.
MINEROLOGY_GANGUE: Hematite  Micaceous,  Iron oxide (non specific),  Limonite

DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: ferruginous outcrop with amorphous graphite, and some flake. The host rock trended 030, with a 10 m section of ferruginous graphitic material recorded. A concentrate had 1.52% flake graphite.

3 m deep pit sunk on decomposed feldspathic schist with a trace of flake graphite. There was a ferruginous capping spangled with flake graphite. The weathered bedrock might be equivalent to banded iron formation, trending NE, dipping 50 NW.

2 horizons containing flake graphite, and trending 340. One horizon occurred in kaolinised schists located between two quartzite layers. The other was associated with chalcedonic quartz and ironstone.

shows of flake graphite in deeply weathered, ferruginous gneiss and quartzite, trend N12E, possibly of the Warrow Quartzite. best value from grab sample of ore material was 9-12% flake graphite at 80-88% total C.
shallow prospecting shaft reported to have been sunk in kaolinised graphitic gneiss.
surface outcrop of blue and white, weathered graphitic schist investigated by drilling. Hole Coomlinga #1 penetrated interlayered marbles and graphitic schist at 149.35-160.45 m.

trenches excavated on an EM anomaly exposing gneiss of the Warrow Quartzite, with disseminated flake graphite. Best value 1.25m interval of 11% total C. The conductive axis of the EM anomaly correlated with the graphitic horizons.
surface rubble of disseminated amorphous graphite rock in host deeply weathered metasediment of the Hutchison Group. Sampling gave an average value of 4.5% flake at 35% total C.

flake graphite in ploughed field strewn with ferruginous graphitic rock. Host schist/gneiss with specular hematite. The graphite was amorphous, content was proportional to the iron oxide content. Samples at 4.5-21.5%C. The host schist trended NE.
mine developed on a low grade to marginal graphite showing in laterite at the surface.
small prospecting pit developed on a surface show of graphite-bearing schist. It was drill tested in holes 83MKRC6 (20 m @ 3.6% C), and 83MKRC7 (20 m @ 2.36% C).
graphite in host Hutchison Group metasediment. Relates to Yarranyacka lode on MC 10617 being a continuation of lode from coastal exposure, mindep #235.
disseminated graphite in host Hutchison Group metasediment. Drill hole confirmed the presence of graphite. Hole 82MKD-11 indicated 8.7 m @ 8.3% C including  2.8 m @ 11.9% C and 7.7 m @ 9.2% C.

Jack (1918) reported a 4m shaft in weathered feldspathic schistose gneiss with rich micaceous graphite. Trench excavated on Section 34, Hundred Sleaford for sample returning value of 8.5% flake graphite size 0.4-1mm.

graphitic rocks in coastal cliffs. Sediments included feldspar schist, quartzite, gneiss, and calc-silicate. The most graphitic rock was a calc-silicate on the western headland. Sampling identified average flake graphite from 4-7%.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: GRAPHITE LTD; ML 5561; ML 5562; OURAY; PIT 2; RL 66; RL 67; S.A. GRAPHITE LTD; ULEY 1; ULEY 3; ULEY 4; ULEY 6; ULEY GRAPHITE SYNDICATE; ULEY MAIN ROAD
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: stratabound zones to 12m thick of >6%C flake graphite in host biotite-quartz schist equated with the Cook Gap Schist. Production from 1986-93 ~1000t. Indicated resources 2.87Mt @ 13% flake graphite.

lead-zinc bearing strata parallel to a magnetic trend investigated by soil geochemical survey. Auger drilling for discouraging results of generally low values for best values 640ppmCu, 1800ppmPb, and 710ppmZn.
horizon of calc-silicate marble of the Katunga Dolomite, and partially serpentinised. Worked seasonally for decorative stone from a shallow quarry from 1979-2003 for production of ~1300 tonne.
minor brannerite confined to hornblende-rich phases in Lincoln Complex hornblende-granitic gneiss concordant to the foliation.
minor brannerite confined to hornblende-rich phases in Lincoln Complex hornblende-granitic gneiss concordant to the foliation.
minor brannerite confined to hornblende-rich phases in Lincoln Complex hornblende-granitic gneiss concordant to the foliation.

amphibolite flow or sill containing disseminated pyrrhotite and pyrite within host sequence of dolomite, and banded iron formation of the Hutchison Group. Samples returned assays of Cu to 1900ppm and Zn to 5600ppm.

stream sediment sample with elevated zinc, followed up by drilling. The holes confirmed Hutchison Group metasediment, in particular host to elevated uranium (9ppm), and thorium (100ppm) was Katunga Dolomite.

horizon of gossanous boxworks in vuggy, epidote quartzite bed adjacent to BIF. Metal values of Pb to 1940 ppm and 3380 ppm Zn were recorded. Veins of chrysotile asbestos to 15mm wide reported in host marble of the Katunga Dolomite.

linear 3km magnetic anomaly on N-plunging F2 regional antiform. Source as magnetite-bearing BIF of Lower Middleback Jaspilite. Inferred resource ~55Mt @ 26.8%DTR for 68.3%Fe product at 75 micron grind. Target additional 60-120Mt.
dolomite outcrop tested for suitability for use as road aggregate and adjacent to bitumen road. Diamond drilling identified inferred resource at the northern site on section 414 of 75,000m3.

southern of two dolomite outcrops tested for suitability for use as road aggregate and located close to the Lipson-Ungarra bitumen road. Diamond drilling identified a deep weathering profile on section 413, no resource estimate attempted.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: A. ELLIOTS CLAIM; B. EDWARDS; BROLGA TALC MINING CO.; C.J. PARTINGTONS CLAIM; COOKES CLAIM; MC 12118; ML 2676; ML 4956; S.A. MINES CO.; YARANYACKA
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: 2 discontinuous, lenticular lines of talc in host marble of the Hutchison Group. Combined past production (1910-56), and remaining resource ~77,000 tonne.
narrow 5 cm wide vein of fibrous asbestos. Later assessment of host marble resource identified 3 prospective marble outcrops of Katunga Dolomite. Asbestos mineral identified as chrysotile.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: MC 8143; MC 8735; MC 8780; PRISK SHAFT; STEPHEN SHAFT; TUMBY LODE
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: number of trial pits from 1-2 m deep. He judged from surface indications that the deposit was large, and of good quality. 41 tonne was dispatched in 1899. The ore consisted of hand picked pyrolusite.
manganese oxide outcrop of ~37m2 in 3 separate exposures in host metamorphic Lincoln Complex host. Prospected in small pits, no production records, resource ~1500 tonne/m for total 10-15Mt.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: CONDELL AND PROVIS; CONDELLS; COPPER KING; COPPERER; FLINDERS; HARRIS HILL; HEYWARDS; KOONA; MC 8144; MONTEZUMA; MOORAHNOO; NEW YEARS GIFT; TUMBY BAY; WHEAL BESSIE
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: Cu mineralisation in 3 EW-trending lodes in host greenish, fine-grained gneiss of Donington Granitoid Suite. Production for 1898-1918 ~185t for 26t copper metal product.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: MC 9303; ML 380; ML 381; ML 453; ML 454; ML 492; ML 493; ML 588; ML 692; ML 699; ML 700; MORTLOCKS; TALC CLAIM 11803
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: shear-hosted Cu-Au mineralisation in quartz breccia in host quartzite and dolomite of the Cook Gap Schist. Later drilling confirmed weak mineralisation at depth, best assay to 1.1%Cu, 0.4 g/t Au.
MINEROLOGY_ORE: Azurite,  Chalcocite,  Chalcopyrite,  Covellite,  Gold,  Malachite

DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: quartz vein in host Donington Suite gneiss, and carrying copper carbonates and sulphides. Large body of chalcocite outcropped at the low tide mark, with associated barren EW cross-cutting quartz stringers.

surface show of malachite in migmatitic metasediment of the Cook Gap Schist, with the foliation trending 030, dipping west. The migmatite contained larger pegmatitic segregations, some with tourmaline.
2 lodes 300m apart, trending EW in host quartz-hornblende schist of the Middleback Subgroup. Recorded production 864t ore, unreliable grade figures 25-30%Cu.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: BOOTHBYS; COPPERINGA; EML 4790; J.C. LYNN; TUMBY BAY MARBLE
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: marble of the Katunga Dolomite, with some serpentine and minor biotite garnet gneiss. The bedding trended 060, dipped 75 NW. A tight drag fold in west wall of pit had the axial plane with the same orientation.

abandoned costean of 250m2 x 1-5m deep on low ridge of deeply weathered metasediment of Hutchison Group, mapped as within the sequence Katunga Dolomite to Lower Middleback Jaspilite. There is a report of magnesite occurring on Section 45.
area of ~7Ha x 1-4m deep worked for road fill. Sequence exposed was surface soil, calcrete over white, weathered to clays gneiss of the Donington Suite.

shear-controlled quartz-Cu vein (similar to Mount Liverpool). Vein trend 030, concordant with the foliation of the host Donington Suite. Mineralisation consisted of copper oxidation products (malachite, azurite) disseminated through the vein-quartz.
quartz veins emplaced within a shear zone. The veins had an anastomising form, and were up to 30 cm wide, with visible crystal terminations in voids
shear-hosted quartz vein carrying Cu mineralisation. Host rock was pegmatite. Incomplete production records of 13t, no records for yields or grades. Large mine dumps implied extensive workings.
bleached and mottled Tertiary weathering zone in sandstone/quartzite of the Warrow Quartzite. Production from 1981-93 was ~1600 tonne for road base material.

interbanded gneiss & amphibolite investigated as source of material for road aggregate in 1984. Resource estimated at 80,000m3 beneath 17,000m3 of soil and clay cover of 2m. Additional reserves available to N & S or at depth.

abandoned council pit of >5,000m2 x 1-4m deep developed on western slope of a NNE-trending strike ridge of >150m width, >600m length, and on weathered sandstone to quartzite of the Warrow Quartzite for road fill material.

shallow scrape <15,000m2 x <1m deep on weathered augen gneiss. Mapping identified black cumulate gabbro, weathered in part. Worked for road aggregate and road fill. The basic plug was anomalous in Ni (as pentlandite?)

road base material from host Burrawing Amphibolite. Associated blue, grey-white banded metasediment trended 025, dipped vertiacl to steep west. The rock was used as aggregate. A cross cutting pegmatite was in the NE corner, and trended 340.

deposit of red and whitte clay as source of brick clay for the Pooninde Brickworks. Clay derived from bleached, weathered zone of Hutchison Group schist of the Burrawing Amphibolite. Production from 1976-80 was estimated at 2200 tonne.

deposit on a lime sand spread worked around 1919 for production of ~70 tonne. The whiting assayed CaCO3 @ 83.64%, MgCO3 @ 8.00%, insolubles @ 1.18%. Workings of shallow pits to 1m. 1928 resource ~20,000 tonne.
low grade whiting deposit noted in the floor of a lake, with CaCO3 65.3%, MgCo3, 26.1%, and insolubles around 4%.
pegmatite containing small (4 cm) beryl crystals. The pegmatite intruded Archean gneiss adjacent to its contact with Proterozoic Warrow Quartzite at a contact on the coast.
zone of thinly disseminated pitchblende mineralisation concordant to foliation in soda of hornblende granitic gneiss.
zone of thinly disseminated pitchblende mineralisation concordant to foliation in soda hornblende granitic gneiss.
zone of thinly disseminated pitchblende mineralisation concordant to foliation in hornblende granitic gneiss of the Donington Suite.
disseminated pitchblende in concordant granitic hornblende gneiss ore body.  400 tons ore at 2kg U3O8/ton.
thinly disseminated pitchblende throughout steeply dipping condcordant hornblende granitic gneiss. 5000t of ore at 0.9 -1.3kg U3O8/ton.
2 adjacent, abandoned, historic pits of total area <5,000m2 x 1-2m deep on Holocene Moornaba Sand. Probable council pits for road fill.
shallow roadside pit of dimensions ~30,000m2 x 1-3m deep developed on Pleistocene sand for material for road fill.

ferruginous laterite on Middleback Iron Formation worked for flux. They failed to penetrate to the underlying BIF. Pillaworta lay along strike from the Koppio iron prospect. The BIF trended NE, dipped 75 SE.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: LADY FRANKLYN; MC 10740; MC 11127; MC 11147; MC 11148; MOONLIGHT
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: blue quartz veins in host talcose, serpentinised shale of the Hutchison Group. ore minerals; galena, sphalerite and minor pyrite, carrying silver and gold. No production figures determined. Later drilling identified sub-economic Au-Pb-Cu-Zn-Ag values.
abandoned quarry with dimensions ~1,000m2 x 1-4m deep developed on weathered metasediment of the Cook Gap Schist. Presumably a local council pit for road fill material.
rehabilitated pit of ~1Ha x 1-3m deep on Pleistocene alluvial sand spread, with estimated production from 1976-83 of ~30,000 tonne.
gravel deposit developed for filling.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: LINCOLN CC#2; PORT LINCOLN CC#2; TRANSPORT SA
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: single bench quarry of ~5,500m2 x 1-10m developed in 1956 on Palaeoproterozoic granitic gneiss primarily for the production of road seal aggregate

irregular shaped area of historic excavations of >10,000m2 x 1-2m deep for sand on deposits marginal to the north shore of a low-lying swamp area. Presumably worked by the local council for road fill.
area of >5,000m2 x 1-2m deep of shallow pits developed by local council on Pleistocene sand for material for road fill.
pit of <15,000m2 x 1-4m deep on Holocene, white, kaolinitic aeolian sand of the Moornaba Sand, and worked for road fill.
southernmost of a series of abandoned and part rehabilitated pits for collective area >7Ha x 1-3m deep over a NS distence of ~1km, and developed on Tertiary ferricrete, for railway ballast.

2 abandoned scrapes of ~5,000m2 x 1-2m deep on Pleistocene limestone and calcrete of the Bridgewater Formation, and worked for road fill. Production record only for early 1979 was 4,500 tonne. The pits were rehabilitated in 1980.
historic quarry >10,000m2 x 1-3m deep on calcrete of the Bridgewater Formation, and worked for road aggregate. Now rehabilitated and partly occupied by industrial premises.
area of historic quarries on limestone of the Bridgewater Formation, and worked for road aggregate. Now rehabilitated, and occupied by housing.
long abandoned pits worked for loam, now a minor, water-filled depression.
site of a long abandoned pit now almost disappeared.

rehabilitated quarry of ~2,000m2 x 1-3m deep developed for road aggregate and road fill on a prominent vein quartz blow. Production from 1982-84 was estimated at 7450 tonne, and rehabilitation was completed in 1988.
shallow quarry of ~3,500m2 x 1-3m deep on deeply weathered, white, kaolinised metasediment of the Warrow Quartzite, and worked for road base material.
historic roadside council quarry ~8,000m2 x 1-4m deep developed on isolated outcrop of deeply weathered metasediment of the Warrow Quartzite, presumably for material for road fill.

historic quarry ~8,000m2 x 1-4m deep adjacent to disused tramway line, and developed on isolated outcrop of deeply weathered metasediment of the Warrow Quartzite, presumably for material for railway fill or ballast and road fill.

2 scrapes ~200m apart NS, with combined area <10,000m2 x 1-3m deep, and developed for road fill material on area of Tertiary ferricrete overlying weathered iron formation of the Lower Middleback Jaspilite..

weathered BIF of Middleback Jaspilite for use as road base material. There was an iron enriched cap of Tertiary age. These host rocks, and the capping were also mined, being used as road base material, and filling.
outcrop of graphitic rock and ironstone of the Middleback Subgroup, and extending for ~1.7 km, striking NE, dipping 65 E. There were large flakes of graphite associated with sugary quartz.

The Graphite in the Kookaburra Gully area occurs within the Paleoproterozoic Hutchison group metasediments that have undergone high grade metamorphism of upper Amphibolite and lower granulite facies, producing coarse grained flake graphite within graphitic schist units which have been multiply folded and/or sheared bordered by major fault zones within the Hutchison group. The folding and ductile shearing has produced a series of lenses. Resource estimate as of 16/04/20245: 3.1Mt @ 11.72% TGC for total of 412,000 tonnes of contained graphite with a 2% cut-off.  primarily schist and gneissic rocks with minimal marble, pegmatite and quartz veins.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: LOCATION 20; MC 359; ML 2861; ML 2948; WESTERN CARBON CO.
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: bed of graphite schist at the contact of an intrusion of aplite into schist and quartzite of the Hutchison Group. Resources estimated in 1945 were 22,600 tonnes @ 12.2%C. Recorded production from 1941-46 was 99 tonnes.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: FUSION; GERMAN GULLY; KOPPIO WEST; ROCK VALLEY CREEK; TOMS WELL
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: 5km linear magnetic anomaly on strike ridges of magnetite-bearing BIF of Hutchison Group. Deeply weathered to 70-80m. Total contained and recoverable iron metal ~36Mt. Deposit of Eyre Iron's Fusion Project.

abandoned quarry <2,000m2 x 1-6m deep on eastern end of a narrow, short (250m), EW-trending strike ridge of deeply weathered white, kaolinitic Warrow Quartzite. Presumably a council quarry developed for road fill material.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: BALIA HILL; KOPPIO; MC 4887; MC 5125; ML 4821
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: amazonite-bearing pegmatite in Lincoln Complex granite gneiss. Pegmatite 0.8m wide, and appeared to occupy a shear zone. A shaft to 4 m depth was excavated, and there were three shallow pits. Production from 1965-66 was recorded at 4 tonne.
deposit of fine to medium quartzite investigated as source of road aggregate. Moderately well developed bedding, platy and sericitic in parts. Resource ~555,000m3.
metasediment variable from compact grey quartzite to micaceous schist, to sugary quartzite of the Warrow Quartzite, resource estimated at >1Mt. .

red-brown to yellow mottled clay becoming whiter at depth, in places up to 2 m thick. They occurred beneath 30-60 cm of ironstone gravel lags. Testwork showed it was not suitable for use in making bricks.

deposit of Quaternary white to yellow-brown sand and clay, tested in single water bore hole for estimated resource of ~120,000 tonne. Later worked by local council in 2 pits ~400m apart for total area >5,000m2 x 1-3m deep for road fill.
deposit of clay tested for brick making, and was determined to have unsuitable milling characteristics.

series of small, long abandoned pits marginal to and south of Tod River, and working a reportedly remarkably uniform deposit of Holocene alluvial clay, free from gravel and lime pockets. No production figure determined. Resource 1964 at 145,300m3.

deposit of quartz-feldspar gneiss assessed for use as railway ballast. It was coarsely banded, bleached, and partly ferruginised, but freshened at shallow depth. resources estimated at 115,000m3 to 235m contour.
dense quartzite assessed for use as ballast. There was a proportion of muscovite flakes, also minor vuggy quartz veins, with tourmaline and muscovite. Resources estimated at 153,000m3.
411 Ibs (154.5kg) of wolfram ore was reported as excavated. Located on the north coast of Langton Island from 1942-44. No trace of the workings remains.
wolfram, tungstite, and scheelite occurred in a quartz lens in host granodiorite.
disseminated sulphides including chalcopyrite, minor sphalerite visible in granodiorite of the Lincoln Complex.
trace of sulphides visible in an amphibolite dyke.

pods, disseminations of molybdenite-scheelite mineralisation was identified along the southern shores in quartz veins and aplitic dykes in host Mesoproterozoic granite.  Global resource estimate 250,000 tonne of 0.25% combined Mo-W.

gypsum deposit of the Holocene Yamba Formation. Drilling on dunal lime sand gave estimated resource of 4.2Mt at 80% gypsum cutoff for grade of 87.8%. Production from 2009-13 for ~28,000 tonne for use in agriculture.

dunal seed gypsum E margin Lake Malata. Drilling for resource of 1.2Mt @ 92.3% CaSO4. Inferred resource >30Mt of 80-90% gypsum beneath salt crust. Production from 1992-2015 ~400,000t plasterboard grade, lesser agricultural use.

deposit of kaolinised granite gneiss, with drilling and testwork carried out from 1973, again in 1986-88. Testwork determined kaolin migh be suitable for paper filler, and possibly for ceramics. Resource ~11Mt in 1973.
pit of <2Ha x 1-2m deep on pale yellow lime sand of the Bridgewater Formation, now rehabilitated an used as a council depot.

3 diamond holes for proven 150,000m3 resource. Local opposition to quarrying so alternative sites inspected. Disadvantaged relative to Moody. Inferior site on coarse porphyritic granite, 6 km to the west was recommended for further investigation.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: EML 5111; EML 5479; EML 5480; PM 181; PORT LINCOLN
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: large open cut on Kirton Point Gneiss for use as aggregate, and crusher fines as artificial sand. Limited volume of cross-cutting amphibolite suitable for road making material. No resource estimate. Production from 1977-2013 ~3.3Mt.
shallow scrapes of ~3,500m2 x 1-2m deep on Pleistocene clays and gravel overlying weathered granite, possibly of the Moreenia Granite, and worked for road fill.

microgranite of the Palaeoproterozoic Lincoln Complex, and yielding ~100,000m3 of material for use as road ballast, and from shallow open cut 100m x 20m x 5m in 1979. Large resources remain to east and west.

granitoid tor ~250m across, located adjacent to the Ungarra-Yeelanna road. It was assessed for use as railway ballast in 1980. Resources were estimated at 150,000m3. There was local resistance to any mining.
abandoned sand pit of <1,000m2 x 1-3m deep on Pleistocene coastal lime sand, and worked by the E&WS for filling sand.
dunal sand of the Moonaba Sand Formation considered too fine for use in concrete, but satisfactory for use as filling sand.
coarse river sands in modern and old creek beds. There were insufficient reserves of coarse sand to sustain long term mining.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: EML 4966; PIONEER CONCRETE SA PL; STRAWBERRY HILL
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: deposit of Tertiary river sand. Production from 1981-2010 exceeded resource estimate, being >80,000 tonne. The pit has been rehabilitated.
river sand in Tertiary Palaeochannel, and suitable for construction sand if washed. Production of 3,000 tonne in 1985. There were limited reserves, possibly better towards Strawberry Hill.
worked a deposit of guano. No production figures were reported.
2.5m thick deposit of well sorted sand suitable for use as construction sand. Located in a creek mouth NE of Lake Wangary, and adjacent to the Flinders Highway. Resource estimated at 250,000 tonne.

shallow pit of ~4Ha x 1-2m deep worked for road fill. Coastal sand dune to the immediate south inspected by the Geological Survey in mid 1970s to identify a resource of 0.8m of fine sand over 1.2m of pale yellow clayey sand sitting on calcrete base.
Pleistocene sand worked in a pit to 1.5m deep, with production from 1973-88 of ~47,500 tonne concrete, building, and garden sand. It has been rehabilitated.

ridge of dunal sand of the Semaphore Sand Member. Resources extended onto section 105. It was mined mainly for concrete sand, but also for construction and filling sand. Production from 1993-2011 was estimated at >40,000 tonne.

DEPOSIT_SYNONYMS: EML 3203; EML 3245; HAGE SAND; LOUTH BAY SAND
DEPOSIT_SUMMARY: fine aeolian Semaphore Sand Member, and mainly used in Port Lincoln as a filler in  superphosphate. Production from 1973-2013 was estimated at 232,000 tonne.

2.5m thick deposit of fine aeolian sand of the Semaphore Sand Member, with overlying 1.2m of coarser more suitable sand. Production from 1973-2009 was estimated at 252,000 tonnes. resource estimate in 1992 of 450,000 tonne.

deposit of lime sand suitable for use as blast furnace flux. The deposit consisted of mobile dunes to 60m high, formed by erosion of the calcareous Bridgewater Formation dune system. Production from 1966-2005 ~3.16Mt.

fossil bone breccia and guano at W end of island circa 1909. Tricalcic phosphate, with values assaying from 54.6-68.3 %. No production figures were recorded, with mention made that a considerable volume had been excavated mixed with sand.
thick but poor quality guano deposit, unworked circa 1909.
guano harvested from shallow pits and trenches on the island circa 1909 for phosphate. estimated 276 tonnes harvested in 1909, remaining resource >7100 tonne.
guano and rock phosphate production circa 1909. Guano was 30-100cm deep, with some sand as impurities. Production ~117 tonne at 30%P, remaining resource in 1909 estimated at 7,000 tonne at 30%P.
1 microdiamond found in a stream sediment sample, with some suggestion of a contaminated sample (Env 04163).
quartz reef referred to in a Mining Review 10 & 11 reports. Gold was reported from a reef 8.5km (5 miles) south of Tarcoola.

small hill of hematite-goethite rock, 3 smaller hills ~1km S. 12 diamond drillholes penetrated variably altered felsic, and mafic gneiss of the Kenella Gneiss. Dating gave an age of 2488 +-130 Ma. Best intersection hole DDH1A, 1.2m at 4.7%Zn.

low hill of Archean, subcropping banded iron formation (BIF), with minor, surficial, massive hematite. Diamond hole CD 3 intersected true thickness of 76 m BIF, Fe to 35%. Estimated resource BIF 2Mt per 30m depth.

low hill of 2 narrow Archean BIF bands. Tested in holes PDH 1-3, which intersected dark grey meta-BIF. Values to 46.8% Fe, with 26.4% SiO2. Weathered ultrabasic possible source of anomalous base metals, Ni (to 1000ppm), Au and REE.

low hills of Archean BIF drill tested in hole CD 5, which intersected BIF from 15-40m. Resource ~400-500,000 tonnes, with best Fe assay at 49.9%. The rocks dipped 80 NNW. There was BIF in another keel structure 300 m north of George Hill.

strike ridge of well laminated meta-BIF of the Mulgathing Complex tested in 2 diamond drillholes. Grade in hole CD1 was 34%Fe from 20-90m. Dry magnetic separation produced concentrate at 56-65%Fe. Global resource estimate of 2.5Mt/30m depth.

hard cap limestone of the Nullarbor limestone. Massive limestone overlying porous friable limestone. The base of capping undulated, and was up to 5m thick. It was deemed not suitable for use with concrete sleepers. Resources ~59,000m3 in 1981.

granite gneiss of the Lincoln Complex assessed for suitability for use as railway ballast. Drilling identified a variable depth of weathering from 0-7m, with some sand overburden. Resource ~434,000m3.
deposit of metasiltstone to metapelite of the Mesoproterozoic Tarcoola Formation quarried for railway ballast. Production was in several phases beginning in 1916, ending in 1979, with total ~1.25Mt.

quarry developed in weakly altered rhyolite of the GRV for use as railway ballast, with undersize material from crushing reprocessed by DTEI. A significant resource of ballast, and road aggregate remains on site.

NNW quartz reefs for 1.7km, visible sulphide. Mineralisation associated with dykes of GRV porphyry, basic intrusive. Sampling gave best values Ag (200-650ppm), Zn (5000 ppm), Pb (1000-2000 ppm), Cu (1000 ppm), and Bi (3000 ppm).

weak Au-(Cu) mineralisation in quartz reefs, some alluvials. Host massive quartzite of the Fabian Quartzite. Exploration identified best surface assay 2.1ppm Au, 1200ppmCu. No significant Au-Cu-U from follow up drilling.
Au-(Pb-Zn) mineralisation in quartz veins in host metasediment of the Tarcoola Formation and also granite. Later RAB drilling identified best value in hole DH031, 5m @ 1.24g/t Au.

quartz lodes in host slate of the Tarcoola Formation to underlying Paxton Granite. A parcel of 6.1 tonnes yielded 49gm gold at 8g/tAu. Later exploration identified minor Cu-Au mineralisation in basal conglomerate, underlying altered granite.

narrow ferruginous quartz vein, which followed a shear zone in the Kenella Gneiss. It was located a few km south of the main Lake Labyrinth workings. No production figure was determined.

cassiterite in 1m wide quartz-feldspar vein in decomposed granite/pegmatite dyke in highly weathered gneiss (Kenella Gneiss). Incomplete production records only of 14kg cassiterite concentrate production in 1943.
thin greisen veins in granite host, average 33 ppmSn, and 15 ppm in granite host. 5 bulk samples returned values from 0.28-0.36%Sn. Mineral was probably cassiterite.

calcreted aeolianite of the Pleistocene Wiabuna Formation quarried for aggregate. Production from 1978-2013 of ~59,000 tonne of calcrete, limestone and sand products, mainly for filling and road base material.
pit of >1Ha x 1-3m deep on calcreted limestone of the Pleistocene Wiabuna Formation, and worked for road base material. Production from 1985-2012 was estimated at 33,000 tonne.
dunal sand of the Holocene Semaphore Sand Member. Production from 1987-2013 was estimated at 27,000 tonne of concrete and garden sand.

sand and limestone deposit in Bridgewater Formation. Sand production from 1985-1997 was >8,000 tonne. Limestone production for filling from EML 5989 from 2008-13 was ~7,000 tonne. The pit is being progressively rehabilitated.
pit developed on vegetated calcareous dunal limestone and sand of the Pleistocene Wiabuna Formation, with production from 1990-2009 estimated at 4,500 tonne limestone for filling.

lease taken out over massive, pink feldspar, phenocrystic Hiltaba Granite with white-green plagioclase for dimension stone, but unworked.
scrape in Quaternary dune sand and creek bed. Production from 1978-2013 was estimated at 5200 tonne of concrete sand.
ferruginous sandstone of the Corraberra Sandstone, honeycomb weathered and case hardened along polygonal joint sets gives rock fragments in demand for ornamental uses. Marketed as aquarium stone.

semi-precious amethystine quartz filled fractures and cavities in quartz body cross-cutting host schist/gneiss. Reef traced for ~10km. Colour variable and multicoloured. Crystals small rarely exceeding 6cm.Proportion of gem-quality <5%.

salt crust to ~30mm thick exploited in a small way, though impurities were high. It was worked from 1917-1919, and 1947- 1949. Recorded production from 1917-39 was estimated at 128,000 tonne. Resources estimated in 1921 were 5Mt.
gossanous carbonate rock of the Amberoona Formation, with chemical analysis returning values of 1150ppm Cu, 150ppm Zn, 650ppm W, 8,600ppm As, 455ppb Au, and 440ppm Bi.
4 zones of replacement-style Pb-Zn-Ag sulphide mineralisation in breccia horizons in host Palaeoproterozoic marble & calc-silicate. Resources ~3.8Mt @ 3.2%Pb, 4%Zn & 34g/tAg.

elevated BMs in Hutchison Group graphitic schist drill tested to identify 2m interval of sulphides, grades 0.34% Pb, and minor Zn, and Ag. The occurrence was thought to be a metamorphosed syngenetic, stratiform origin of the Broken Hill type.
Tertiary ferruginous gravels for road foundations. Unsorted, variously cemented. Production of concrete sand product from 1977-2004 was estimated at 10,100 tonne.
2 roadside pits ~500m apart on Gawler Ranges Road developed on Tertiary gravel used for road foundations. 1.2m of alluvium overlay 1.2m of exposed Tertiary.
series of lakes and dunes containing gypsum of the Holocene Yamba Formation have been formed in the Corrobinnie Depression.

outcrop of dark green metamorphosed diopside-tremolite-garnet marble worked for jade in a shallow bulldozer scrape for a short period in the 1970s, though no production recorded.
area of deeply weathered, kaolinised basement rock tested by drilling. Results indicated a low-grade resource requiring extensive processing to meet paper coating standards.
trace of chromite found in heavy mineral fraction in creek bed draining off GRV's.
trace of chromite found in a heavy mineral fraction in a creek bed draining off the Gawler Range Volcanics.
microdiamond 0.2 x 0.175mm found in heavy mineral segment of creek gravels by CRA Exploration PL in the mid 1980s.
broad low grade U anomaly in Tertiary Narlaby Palaeochannel associated with complex series of redox fronts.
anomalous radioactivity (>10 000 cps) at interface of humic mud horizon and haematitic sandstones and clays.

kaolinised bedrock formed by intense surface weathering of gneiss of the Lincoln Complex, drilling identified kaolin quality was variable and below that required for high-grade kaolin markets.

drilling identified minor Zn-Pb mineralisation in host Cook Gap Schist amphibolite, best value 1.18%Zn over 2m. The mineralised interval was converse to the magnetic susceptibility.

amphibole-garnet schist of the Hutchison Group, and with disseminated sulphides. Drilling identified Zn>Pb mineralisation, with values of 5m >1%Zn. Zn was associated with pyritic metachert horizons, probably representing an exhalite.

drillhole DDH C1, with weak, stratiform, banded, disseminated scheelite mineralisation. Follow-up drilling indicated no extent to mineralisation.

shear-hosted hematite rock for strike length ~1100 m. 2 parallel EW-trending narrow zones. Resource of main zone ~210,000 tonnes per 30 m depth, with surface samples grading 37.5-55% Fe. Centrex collected surface samples in 2009 of 37-55%Fe.
council roadside quarry ~1,500m2 x 1-3m deep developed on deeply weathered dolomite of the Katunga Dolomite. It was reported that several lithology types were exposed in the quarry.
many small lakebed, and lake shoreline dune occurrences of bedded gypsite, gypsarenite, and selenite strata of an acceptable grade and thickness for agricultural use. Resources ~4.2Mt at 88% gypsum.
large, low dune about 800m long of flour and seed gypsum bordering a main road. A brief examination included prospecting pits and 2 drill holes. A resource of 44,000 tonne was estimated.
gypsarenite dunes blown up from a lakebed, and mined for agricultural and plasterboard gradesuses. Production from 1987-2015 was estimated at 105,000 tonne.
shallow prospecting pit on a zone of copper mineralisation (azurite) at a granite/aplite contact with host iron formation. Sample returned 1%Cu. Page 17, envelope 1108.

quartz veins with silver-bearing slugs of galena. Cross-cut a deeply weathered mica schist/slate over a width of 12-15m. It was prospected via a small trench, and several pits and shallow shafts in 1887. Samples returned values to maximum 134g/tAg.
lode 1.2m wide of quartz malachite and azurite in mica Yadnarie Schist. The lode crosscut the schist, dipped 50N.
anomalous Zn-bearing pyritic gossanous zones to 1980ppm detected in Hutchison Group ironstone and calc-silicate horizons. Not considered of enough significance to warrant further work.

copper carbonate hosted by ferruginous amphibolite outcrop of the Cook Gap Schist. Bunches of copper carbonate in a brecciated quartz vein associated with gossanous hematite with boxworks. The amphibolite was located within the Cook Gap Schist.
historical prospecting shaft for graphite on Upper Middleback Jaspilite. Later drilling identified anomalous base metals. Drill hole SE of shaft identified Pb to 9000ppm in pyritic schist.
untested surface exposure of graphitic schist of the Yadnarie Schist, and on the upper slopes of a hill.

micaceous Warrow Quartzite with 2-bench quarry on the flank of Tooligie Hill operated on a campaign basis. Production from 1968-74 estimated at 254,000 tonnes. resource estimate 680,000 tonne in 1969.
Pleistocene clayey sand from a lacustrine or beach environment, and below a calcrete horizon. It was drill tested for heavy minerals, and returned minor rutile and zirconium content in the sands.

outcrop of surface enriched Middleback BIF, with assays to 51% Fe. Strike extension to the NW was drill tested in CP holes, which identified anomalous base metals, best values 2700ppmPb, 1890ppmZn, 3.5ppmAg.

minor accumulation of heavy mineral sands on several beaches. The sands were located within a conservation park. Reported analysis was ilmenite 50-55%, and magnetite 30-40%, and thought to be sourced from neighbouring diorite.

broad area of low grade U mineralisation in palaeochannel sediments associated with redox fronts. Best values recorded over 8m interval at 626ppm U3O8, including 1m at 1462ppm U3O8.

workings on pegmatite in Hiltaba Granite, with high amounts of bright red feldspar, and pegmatitic phases with high iron oxide content. Grab samples from mine spoils assayed low Au. Sampling in 2008 identified anomalous REE, notably La and Ce.

saprolitic kaolin analysed was not of a sufficient grade for use as paper filler or coating. Further testing to determine suitability for lower grade applications. The weathered basement had between 1-22 m of kaolinisation.

up to 48 m thickness of kaolinitic clay was penetrated during the drilling. Samples were tested for paper coating quality. Brightness was adequate, but viscosity was unsuitable. Further testing was recommended.
kaolin located while drilling for uranium. Best intersection was 12 m. Highest brightness averaged 85. Best -2 micron yield averaged 30%

programme of diamond drilling indicating that hard compact kunkar at the Wandana locality was too thin for use as rail ballast.
large surficial spread of close-to-shore, unconsolidated calcareous sand dunes sampled for use as a lime sand flux.

beach sands with minor heavy minerals. The sands were not regarded as prospective for hosting an economic resource of heavy minerals. Samples returned 3.42% heavy minerals, being 75% ilmenite, 15% magnetite, and 3% zircon.
drill holes identified profile of kaolinitic, deeply weathered basement rock to 39m depth developed on Mesoproterozoic granite. It was reported as of poor quality.

coarse quartz beach sand replenished naturally. High sphericity, with 5-10 % feldspar, and shell and calcrete impurities. Production from 1968-2000 was estimated at 4225 tonnes. Resource estimate in 1990 of 70,000m3 at 95%SiO2.

gypsum dunes scattered over a dry lake bed. Gypsum represents reworked aeolian dunes, and contained up to 85% gypsum. Production from 1989-2015 was estimated at 11,800 tonne. !986 resource ~851,300 tonne at 85% gypsum.

minor heavy mineral sands, being a single 5-10 cm thick zone below 25 cm of sand, being 20% opaques, mostly ilmenite, 10% zircon, 4% garnet, and 1% rutile, trace also of staurolite, andalusite, epidote, tourmaline. No resource estimate.

shallow prospecting of a large quartz blow with visible arsenopyrite. It was concordant to the bedding/cleavage of host metasediment of the Tapanappa Formation trending NE, dip 45SE. Sampling detected trace gold only.

series of quartz-tourmaline reefs trending EW & parallel to the strike of host Kanmantoo Group quartz-mica schist. One reef was prospected in a small pit from which recovery of gold was reported. Later sampling reported no gold values.
shallow council roadside scrape of >15,000m2 x 1-3m deep on sheet to rubbly Pleistocene Ripon Calcrete, and developed for material for road fill.

1890s prospecting pits near the top of the Cygnet Fault scarp located ~5km west of Kohinoor Mine. Host was poorly bedded, blocky siltstone to fine, silicified sandstone, with abundant disseminated pyrite.
backfilled prospecting pit. No further information, but presumably geological setting similar to that of the Kohinoor mine.
located near lighthouse on wave cut platform. Occurrence of small flakes of molybdenite in granite. There was an unsubstantiated report of a prospecting pit.
unworked Quaternary gypsarenite on a salt lake. resource estimate in 1989 of 142,000 m3 at 85% gypsum.

heavy mineral sand recognised in 1956 on current beach line, and 3 other separate beach levels. Resource estimate 120Mt at 0.03%HM for 429,000 tonne product. Production in early 1970s of ~1,200 tonnes rutile, and 190 tonnes zircon.

minor workings on 3 parallel quartz veins 20m apart that followed the hinge of a parasitic fold on a regional anticline. Sulphides were reported along host bedding planes. No gold was visible in the lode, and later Au & Ag analyses were low.

gold associated with 1-3m wide concordant shear in host mylonite. Incomplete production record for 7.9 tonne yielding 50gm gold at 6.3g/tAu. Later sampling gave 1.05ppm over a 4.4m lode width. Drilling showed no anomalous gold.

silver-lead sulphides associated with a minor brecciated, and re-silicified quartz veins in host Balquhidder Formation. A field inspection in 1990 failed to recognise any sulphides. It was prospected via a small pit/collapsed shaft.

complex quartz lode 10-15m wide in host siltstone, sandstone of Kanmantoo Group. Drilled for best value 1320ppmPb, 3385ppmZn. Regional stream sediment sampling indicated anomalous Pb-Zn extending several km to W and SW.
show of silver-lead ore in host Tunkalilla Formation as recorded by R.g. Sprigg in 1954 and recorded on 1"" to 4 mile geology map, but not found on ground in 1990.

secondary lead-silver mineralisation in quartz veining in major shear zone. The vein showed termination quartz crystals. No mineralisation was seen in 1990. prospected via a single underlie shaft to 11 m depth, now partially infilled (1990).
numerous diggings for ~2km along Eleanor River, with gold associated with minor heavy minerals, some of gem quality. No production figures were determined.
